findings.current: According to the story, he suddenly attained enlightenment while training on this cliff and unleashed a martial art. The force of that One Strike blasted a hole through the bottom of the cliff.
findings.defect: The draft turns the cave opening at the base of the cliff into a hole blasted through the cliff’s bottom, altering the described geometry and mechanism.
findings.rationale: 절벽 밑이 뻥 뚫렸다 means the base or area beneath the cliff was blown open, creating the training cave entrance; it does not describe a hole passing through the cliff’s bottom.
findings.replacement: According to the story, he suddenly attained enlightenment while training on this cliff and unleashed his martial arts, blasting open the base of the cliff with One Strike.
findings.source: 전해지기로는 이 절벽에서 수련하시던 도중 문득 깨달음을 얻어 무공을 펼쳤는데, 일격에 절벽 밑이 뻥 뚫렸다는군.

findings.current: The dirt-covered monster who had suddenly become a dead man staggered to his feet.
findings.defect: The draft calls the figure a literal monster and says he became a dead man, whereas the source calls him a strange figure who was abruptly taken for dead.
findings.rationale: 괴인 denotes a strange or mysterious person here, while 죽은 놈이 되어 버린 refers humorously to the guards having treated him as dead, not to an actual transformation.
findings.replacement: The dirt-covered stranger who had suddenly been written off as dead staggered to his feet.
findings.source: 졸지에 죽은 놈이 되어 버린 흙투성이의 괴인이 비틀거리며 일어났다.

findings.current: “Brother, Third Young Master? What in the world are you talking about?”
findings.defect: The generic address obscures the established senior-to-junior hierarchy: Hong is addressing Childeuk as his younger brother, not addressing an elder or equal.
findings.rationale: 아우 is specifically the older man’s address for a younger male after telling Childeuk to call him hyung; preserving that direction maintains their comic, newly established hierarchy.
findings.replacement: “Little brother, the Third Young Master? What in the world are you talking about?”

findings.current: Its limbs hung limp, and blood streamed from the back of its head, which lay facedown on the ground.
findings.defect: The relative clause grammatically says the back of the head itself was lying facedown rather than the body.
findings.rationale: The source describes the apparent corpse lying facedown with blood flowing from the back of its head.
findings.replacement: Its limbs lay limp, and blood streamed from the back of its head as it lay facedown on the ground.
findings.source: 축 늘어진 사지, 엎어진 뒤통수에서는 핏물이 줄줄 흘러내렸다.

findings.current: Oh, right. These two uncles were here, too.
findings.defect: “Uncles” is an unnatural kinship calque for the narrator’s casual reference to two unrelated older men.
findings.rationale: 아저씨들 is colloquial here and marks the men as older without asserting a family relationship.
findings.replacement: Oh, right. Those two older guys were here, too.

findings.current: “Ugh! It’s a jiangshi! A jiangshi has appeared!”
findings.defect: The explanatory jiangshi footnote is never referenced, leaving an unused Markdown footnote definition.
findings.rationale: 강시 is a culturally specific creature for which the existing concise footnote is useful; adding the marker at its first meaningful occurrence makes the note functional.
findings.replacement: “Ugh! It’s a jiangshi! A jiangshi[^1] has appeared!”

findings.defect: The unlisted proper name 태초 is romanized without translating or explaining its meaningful Korean name.
findings.rationale: Because Taecho is not an established ledger rendering, its first occurrence needs a concise linguistic note rather than unexplained romanization.

findings.current: [^1]: A jiangshi is a reanimated corpse from Chinese folklore, often depicted as a hopping vampire.
findings.defect: The draft lacks the footnote definition required by the newly introduced, unlisted name Taecho Village.
findings.rationale: A brief, spoiler-free definition preserves the Korean name while conveying the meaning that would otherwise be lost in romanization.
findings.replacement:
[^1]: A jiangshi is a reanimated corpse from Chinese folklore, often depicted as a hopping vampire.

[^2]: *Taecho* means “primordial” or “the beginning.”

summary: Several fidelity, hierarchy, terminology, and Markdown issues are actionable.
